# Advanced structure diagnosis

These tasks are about choosing what information must remain available after
many operations. The right structure follows from the query contract.
At this level, one structure is often not enough: coordinates may be
compressed before a Fenwick tree is built; a tree may be flattened before
range updates are applied; heavy-light decomposition may turn a path into
several segment-tree ranges; persistence may add a version dimension.

Describe the solution as a pipeline from original objects, through a
representation change and maintained invariant, to a query decomposition.

# Representation changes

## Coordinate compression

Compression replaces each relevant value by its rank among all relevant
values. It preserves equality and order, not numerical distance. It is safe
for questions such as `value <= x`, but not for formulas needing actual gaps
unless those gaps are stored separately. Include future update values while
collecting coordinates.

## Flattening a rooted tree

An Euler entry order gives every subtree one contiguous interval:

```text
subtree(v) <-> [tin[v], tout[v]]
```

DFS completely finishes one child subtree before entering the next sibling.
That fact proves contiguity. Subtree operations become array-range operations.
A general path is not contiguous in Euler order.

## Heavy-light decomposition

Choose the child with largest subtree as heavy. Heavy edges form contiguous
chains. A root path crosses only `O(log n)` light edges: crossing a light edge
upward at least doubles the subtree size. A path therefore becomes
`O(log n)` array ranges, producing `O(log^2 n)` operations with an ordinary
segment tree.

# Time as another dimension

## Reverse processing

Deletions are often hard while insertions are easy. If operations are known
offline, start from the final state and add deleted objects back in reverse.
Connectivity deletions can then become ordinary DSU unions. Track the
timeline carefully: the reverse state before undoing an operation matches the
forward state after that operation.

## Persistence

A persistent structure retains old versions. A point update copies only one
root-to-leaf path while untouched subtrees are shared:

```text
old root ---- unchanged subtree
       \
        copied path ---- changed leaf
       /
new root ---- same unchanged subtree
```

A persistent segment-tree point update creates `O(log n)` nodes instead of
copying the array. Every root represents one immutable snapshot; shared nodes
must never be mutated.

# Structures inside structures

Value-filtered and two-dimensional queries often use an outer decomposition
by position and an inner sorted list or Fenwick structure by value. A
merge-sort tree stores every element in `O(log n)` sorted node lists. A range
count visits `O(log n)` nodes and binary-searches each list, giving
`O(log^2 n)` query time and `O(n log n)` memory.

For sparse points, compress only coordinates that occur. A full coordinate
grid is impossible when coordinates are large even if the number of points is
small. Always calculate both the number of outer nodes visited and the cost
of each inner operation.

# Deriving a sufficient invariant

Suppose paths support addition and maximum queries. A lazy segment-tree node
needs:

```text
maximum = maximum actual value in this segment
lazy    = uniform addition still owed to its descendants
```

Applying `delta` to a fully covered node adds it to both fields. Pushing sends
the pending addition to the children before a partial descent. Heavy-light
decomposition identifies the ranges; the lazy tree maintains them. These are
separate correctness obligations.

Order statistics instead need counts. During a k-th-element descent, the
left count decides whether to enter the left child or subtract that count and
enter the right. The same logic works on the difference between two
persistent frequency roots when that difference represents a requested
subarray.

# Proof template for composed solutions

Verify a multi-layer solution through small claims:

1. The representation maps every original query to the claimed ranges or
   versions.
2. Every stored node or prefix has a precise invariant.
3. Every update preserves that invariant.
4. Query combination counts each required object exactly once.
5. The number of pieces and cost per piece imply the stated complexity.

Do not replace these claims by “the data structure is standard.” Most bugs
occur between two individually standard techniques.

# Invariant-oriented testing

| Feature | Adversarial shape |
|---|---|
| tree decomposition | chain, star, and balanced branches |
| compression | duplicates and future update values |
| persistence | update an old version after newer ones exist |
| reverse time | delete and restore a critical bridge |
| lazy paths | overlapping full paths and single vertices |
| sparse coordinates | points near both numerical extremes |

Large tests must also exert the intended complexity. A chain exposes linear
parent climbing and recursion depth; alternating path endpoints exercise
heavy-light chain changes; many versions verify that updates copy only
logarithmically many nodes.

# Complete local contest set

| Problem | Title |
|---|---|
| A | Dynamic Order Statistics |
| B | Range Assign and Add |
| C | Static Rectangle Count |
| D | Nested Ranges Count |
| E | Subtree Add, Point Query |
| F | Dynamic Path Maximum |
| G | Subtree Value Count |
| H | Connectivity Countdown |
| I | Persistent Version Sums |
| J | Subtree K-th Smallest |
| K | Sparse Rectangle Sums |
| L | Path Add, Path Maximum |

Problems A--F establish the core coverage. Problems G--L deliberately increase
in difficulty, moving from static range indexing to reversed time, persistence,
sparse two-dimensional indexing, and lazy heavy-light decomposition.

# Model the operations first

For each local problem, list every update and query, then answer:

```text
Is the input static or dynamic?
Does a query ask for an aggregate, a position, or a count of objects?
Can coordinates be compressed without changing comparisons?
Can queries be processed offline?
What information must an internal node or prefix preserve?
```

Do not turn this into a lookup table from wording to structure. Derive an
invariant that would let a proposed representation answer every operation.
The editorial contains the local construction after you have tested yours.

# Prove and test the invariant

State the meaning of each stored number in one sentence. Show how an update
preserves it, and why the query combines stored values into exactly the desired
answer. Test against a slow vector or nested-loop oracle on tiny random cases,
especially repeated values, empty ranges, and coordinates near boundaries.

# Cost accounting

Give both per-operation and total complexity. Include preprocessing,
compression, sorting, and memory. A logarithmic query can still be unsuitable
if a hidden rebuild happens for every operation.

# Exercises

For A through L, write an operation contract and an invariant before coding.
Also name one boundary case your brute-force oracle must include. Consult the
editorial only after this attempt. Solve G--L in order: the progression is part
of the exercise design.
